\section[a vantagem]{a vantagem — the advantage}

\label{lesson:PT-C345-vantagem}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for objective, then the Portuguese for subjective.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a vantagem}
\textbf{a vantagem} — \textquotedblleft{}the advantage\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A grande vantagem desta casa é o jardim.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The great advantage of this house is the garden.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Tirar vantagem de} — to take advantage of.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{vantagem} is usually traced to Old French \emph{avantage}, built on \emph{avant} \textquotedblleft{}before\textquotedblright{}, which EtymDB derives from Late Latin \emph{abante} \textquotedblleft{}before, in front\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{ab} and \emph{ante} \textquotedblleft{}before\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB, Lewis \& Short); Portuguese dropped the first \emph{a-}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a vantagem}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a vantagem}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a vantagem}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for objective, then the Portuguese for subjective, then say \emph{a vantagem} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a vantagem mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The advantage\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a desvantagem]{a desvantagem — the disadvantage}

\label{lesson:PT-C345-desvantagem}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for subjective, then the Portuguese for the advantage.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a desvantagem}
\textbf{a desvantagem} — \textquotedblleft{}the disadvantage\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A desvantagem é que fica longe do centro.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The disadvantage is that it is far from the centre.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Estar em desvantagem} — to be at a disadvantage.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desvantagem} is built from \emph{des-} and \emph{vantagem} \textquotedblleft{}advantage\textquotedblright{}, which is usually traced to Old French \emph{avantage}, on \emph{avant}, from Late Latin \emph{abante} \textquotedblleft{}before\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{ante} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[o aspeto]{o aspeto — the aspect, the side; the appearance}

\label{lesson:PT-C345-aspeto}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the advantage, then the Portuguese for the disadvantage.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o aspeto}
\textbf{o aspeto} — \textquotedblleft{}the aspect, the side; the appearance\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Há um aspeto que ainda não discutimos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There is one aspect we have not discussed yet.}
\end{quote}

European \emph{aspeto} (AO90); Brazil \emph{aspecto}. \emph{Ter bom aspeto} — to look good.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{aspeto} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{aspectus} \textquotedblleft{}a seeing, a sight, an appearance\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{aspicere} \textquotedblleft{}to behold\textquotedblright{}, built from \emph{ad} and \emph{specere} \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[a crítica]{a crítica — the criticism; the review (of a film or a book)}

\label{lesson:PT-C345-critica}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the disadvantage, then the Portuguese for the aspect.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a crítica}
\textbf{a crítica} — \textquotedblleft{}the criticism; the review (of a film or a book)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ele não aceita bem as críticas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He does not take criticism well.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Fazer uma crítica} — to criticise; \emph{o crítico} — the critic.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{crítica} is a learned word from Greek \emph{kritik\'{\={e}}} \textquotedblleft{}the art of judging\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{krínein} \textquotedblleft{}to separate, to judge\textquotedblright{}; Latin borrowed the adjective as \emph{criticus} \textquotedblleft{}fit for deciding\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[ponderar]{ponderar — to weigh up, to consider carefully}

\label{lesson:PT-C345-ponderar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the aspect, then the Portuguese for the criticism.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ponderar}
\textbf{ponderar} — \textquotedblleft{}to weigh up, to consider carefully\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ponderei bem antes de mudar de casa.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I thought it over carefully before moving house.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Ponderar os prós e os contras} — to weigh up the pros and cons.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ponderar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{ponderāre} \textquotedblleft{}to weigh a thing, to ponder\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB, Lewis \& Short), built on \emph{pondus, ponderis} \textquotedblleft{}weight\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
